title: Mission Specialists: A Submersible Under No Flag, and Two Federal Boards That Called the Loss Preventable
participants: U.S. Coast Guard Marine Board of Investigation

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The fares are taken, and the people who pay them are given a job title. OceanGate carries its paying clients as "mission specialists" — in its own Project Execution Plan for the 2023 expedition, "guests who help fund OceanGate" who are assigned tasks aboard. A former operations technician, once a Coast Guard engineering technician himself, tells the chief executive "... you can't just change the title of a person when you're receiving compensation", and resigns citing "the legality of how it [OceanGate] was operating". The NTSB puts the purpose on the record: it notes "OceanGate's intent to avoid safety oversight by assigning tasks to those paying to ride".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The hull is never established as strong enough. The NTSB finds OceanGate's engineering process produced a carbon fibre composite pressure vessel "that contained multiple anomalies and failed to meet necessary strength and durability requirements", and that because the company did not adequately test it, it "was unaware of the pressure vessel's actual strength and durability, which was likely much lower than their target", including how storage condition and towing bore on the vessel's integrity.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Nothing is watching, and the one instrument that was is misread. The Titan flies no flag: it "was not registered in any US state, documented by the US National Vessel Documentation Center, nor inspected by any flag state", and its flag, port of registry, IMO number and classification society are all recorded as not applicable, with the title held by a US company and the operation run from The Bahamas. Its real-time monitoring system generated the data that would have condemned the hull, and the analysis was flawed, so "the company was unaware that the Titan was damaged and needed to be immediately removed from service after dive 80".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The arrangement holds because the rules do not reach it. At the time of the Coast Guard's 1993 guidance for passenger-carrying submersibles, vessels like the Titan — six or fewer passengers — were treated as "uninspected" rather than small passenger vessels, and that guidance was in any case voluntary; the operator never registered or documented the Titan in the United States, nor arranged Coast Guard inspection. The guidance it did not follow advised keeping operations within the depth at which rescue assistance is effective; the Titan dove to the Titanic, far beyond any available rescue, routinely with none standing by, as on the day it was lost.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Two federal boards report, and both say it did not have to happen — which is not the same as anyone answering for it. The NTSB's probable cause is OceanGate's inadequate engineering process, with voluntary guidance and small passenger vessel regulations "insufficient to ensure OceanGate adhered to established industry standards" as contributing. The Coast Guard board's chair says "This marine casualty and the loss of five lives was preventable", and its more than 300 pages add a toxic workplace culture, an inadequate domestic and international regulatory framework, and an ineffective whistleblower process under the Seaman's Protection Act, with 17 recommendations. The NTSB states expressly that it does not determine whether any conduct violated statutory or regulatory requirements; and the Coast Guard's recommendations were, when published, still with the Commandant awaiting a Final Action Memorandum — the gap each board identified left open by the documents that identified it.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The shape this atlas has tracked since 1912: a novel vessel no classification society has passed, a safety standard that is advisory rather than binding, and a class of passenger defined so as to fall outside the protective rule. Here it is the definition that does the work, not a liability cap — the people who paid were entered as participants in the mission.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The unflagged commercial submersible: title in one company, operation from another jurisdiction, no flag state, no class society, no certificate of inspection, and the paying passengers recorded as crew-adjacent "mission specialists" — a deep-ocean passenger operation standing entirely outside the regime written for passenger vessels.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The fares fund the expeditions, and the title given the people paying them is what keeps the oversight those fares would have triggered from attaching. The hull nobody certified is tested by diving it; the monitoring data that would have taken it out of service is read by the company that owns it; and the cost of the error falls on the five people inside.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Titan was lost to the unforgiving deep — a freak accident at 3,800 metres that no rule could have prevented — or, in the other direction, that one reckless chief executive explains the whole of it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Neither survives the two reports. The hull was already damaged before the casualty dive: the NTSB found delamination after dive 80 and further damage of unknown origin after dive 82, and found that the company's own real-time monitoring data meant the Titan "needed to be immediately removed from service after dive 80" — so the failure was recorded in advance, not unforeseeable. And both boards found the framework itself insufficient, the Coast Guard board recommending that the Oceanographic Research Vessel designation be restricted for submersibles and that inspection requirements be extended to all submersibles on commercial or scientific dives — findings about a regime, not about one man's temperament.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: NTSB Marine Investigation Report MIR-25-36: probable cause OceanGate's inadequate engineering process, contributed to by insufficient voluntary guidance and small passenger vessel regulations and by the company's flawed reading of its own monitoring data; the Titan recorded as not registered in any US state, not documented by the National Vessel Documentation Center and not inspected by any flag state, with no IMO number and no classification society; the "mission specialist" framing taken from OceanGate's own Project Execution Plan, with the NTSB noting the company's "intent to avoid safety oversight by assigning tasks to those paying to ride"; and the US Coast Guard Marine Board of Investigation's report of 5 August 2025, more than 300 pages and 17 recommendations, whose chair called the loss of five lives preventable, and which remained under review by the Commandant pending a Final Action Memorandum.

citations.title: National Transportation Safety Board, Hull Failure and Implosion of Submersible Titan, North Atlantic Ocean, June 18, 2023 — Marine Investigation Report NTSB/MIR-25-36 (investigation DCA23FM036)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded and read (text extracted from the official PDF). Section 3.2 states: "The National Transportation Safety Board determines that the probable cause of the hull failure and implosion of the submersible Titan was OceanGate's inadequate engineering process, which failed to establish the actual strength and durability of the Titan pressure vessel and resulted in the company operating a carbon fiber composite vessel that sustained delamination damage that was subsequently exacerbated by additional damage of unknown origin, resulting in a damaged internal structure that subsequently led to a local buckling failure of the pressure vessel. Contributing were US and international voluntary guidance and US small passenger vessel regulations that were insufficient to ensure OceanGate adhered to established industry standards. Also contributing was OceanGate's flawed analysis of their pressure vessel monitoring system data, which led to their continued operation of a damaged pressure vessel." The report records that Titan was owned by Cyclops II Inc and operated by OceanGate Expeditions, based in The Bahamas, both affiliates of OceanGate Inc; that "The Titan was not registered in any US state, documented by the US National Vessel Documentation Center, nor inspected by any flag state"; and in its vessel particulars table that flag, port of registry, official number, IMO number and classification society are all "N/A", with year built 2020. On the paying passengers it records that OceanGate referred to its clients as "mission specialists", described in the company's "Project Execution Plan" for the 2023 expedition as "guests who help fund OceanGate", and in a footnote states: "While the NTSB does not determine whether specific operator conduct violates statutory or regulatory requirements that may be the subject of enforcement by the US Coast Guard, we note OceanGate's intent to avoid safety oversight by assigning tasks to those paying to ride." It records a former operations technician's statement to the CEO that "... you can't just change the title of a person when you're receiving compensation", his resignation citing "the legality of how it [OceanGate] was operating", and his account that the CEO said "if the [US] Coast Guard became a problem ... he would buy himself a congressman and make it go away" — statements of a witness as the report records them, not findings of the Board. On the regulatory framework it records that at the time of NVIC 05-93 (July 1993) "submersibles carrying six or fewer passengers (like the Titan) were considered uninspected vessels--not small passenger vessels", that after the Passenger Vessel Safety Act of 1993 "the definition of a small passenger vessel changed to include any submersible carrying at least one passenger for hire", and that "OceanGate did not register or document the Titan in the United States, nor did they arrange to have it inspected by the US Coast Guard." The report determines probable cause; it does not determine liability.

citations.title: National Transportation Safety Board, investigation DCA23FM036 — Hull Failure and Implosion of Submersible Titan (investigation summary page)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in the browser. The Board's own summary: "On June 18, 2023, about 1047 local time, while diving to the wreck of the ocean liner Titanic in the North Atlantic Ocean, about 372 miles southeast of St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, the submersible Titan's pressure hull failed, and the vessel imploded. All five persons on board the vessel died." It states the damage sequence — damage after dive 80 "in the form of one or more delaminations", further damage of unknown origin after dive 82, and a local buckling failure on the casualty dive (dive 88) — and that "OceanGate's analysis of Titan pressure vessel real-time monitoring data was flawed, so the company was unaware that the Titan was damaged and needed to be immediately removed from service after dive 80." It records that had OceanGate followed NVIC 05-93 guidance for emergency response plans, emergency response assets would likely have been standing by and the Titan found sooner "even though a rescue was not possible in this case", and that despite OceanGate's failure to notify search and rescue assets, "the US Coast Guard's search and rescue coordination efforts were effective". It also states that "voluntary guidance and current US small passenger vessel regulations are not sufficiently tailored to current pressure vessel for human occupancy (PVHO) operations". It gives the Titan's value, with its launch and recovery system, as about $5.6 million CAD per a 2023 customs declaration. A summary page, not the full report; the probable-cause wording is taken from the report itself.

citations.title: U.S. Coast Guard, "Coast Guard Marine Board of Investigation releases report on Titan submersible", press release, 5 August 2025
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on the Coast Guard's official news site. Announces that the Marine Board of Investigation released its Report of Investigation on 5 August 2025 into the loss of the Titan, "which imploded during a June 2023 dive to the Titanic, killing five people", and that the "more than 300-page ROI" carries 17 safety recommendations. Quotes MBI chair Jason Neubauer: "This marine casualty and the loss of five lives was preventable," and his statement that the two-year investigation identified "multiple contributing factors" and that "There is a need for stronger oversight and clear options for operators who are exploring new concepts outside of the existing regulatory framework." States that "The board determined the primary contributing factors were OceanGate's inadequate design, certification, maintenance and inspection process for the Titan", with other factors including "a toxic workplace culture at OceanGate, an inadequate domestic and international regulatory framework for submersible operations and vessels of novel design, and an ineffective whistleblower process under the Seaman's Protection Act"; and that the board found OceanGate "failed to properly investigate and address known hull anomalies following its 2022 Titanic expedition", took no action on real-time monitoring data that "should have been analyzed and acted on", and did not conduct preventative maintenance or properly store the Titan over the extended off season. Recommendations listed include "restricting the Oceanographic Research Vessel designations for submersibles, expanding federal and international requirements to all submersibles conducting scientific or commercial dives and requiring Coast Guard documentation for all U.S. submersibles", and working with the International Maritime Organization "to define passenger submersibles". Records that "The Marine Board's report is now under review by the Commandant of the Coast Guard" and that a Final Action Memorandum will follow. The ROI PDF linked from this page is served from media.defense.gov, which returns 403 to scripted requests and triggers a download rather than rendering in a browser: the report itself was not read here, and nothing above is taken from it beyond what this press release states.
